must_remember: The EMF of a cell is the terminal potential difference when no current is drawn, representing the work done by non-electrostatic forces to move unit positive charge through the entire circuit.
Terminal potential difference $V = E - Ir$ during discharging and $V = E + Ir$ during charging of the cell.
Local action is caused by impurities like iron particles in commercial zinc plates, preventable by amalgamation with mercury.
Polarization is caused by the accumulation of hydrogen gas bubbles on the positive copper electrode, mitigated using depolarizers like manganese dioxide ($MnO_2$).
The condition for maximum power transfer from a source of cells to an external load is when the external resistance equals the total internal resistance ($R = r$).
In series combination of $n$ identical cells, current is given by $I = \frac{nE}{R + nr}$, best suited for large external resistance.
In parallel combination of $m$ identical cells, current is given by $I = \frac{mE}{mR + r}$, best suited for small external resistance.

glossary.meaning: The maximum potential difference across the terminals of a cell when it is in an open circuit condition ($E$).
The opposition offered by the electrolyte and electrodes of a cell to the flow of internal ions ($r$).
A chemical defect in primary cells caused by metallic impurities in the zinc plate forming local voltaic cells.
A defect caused by the deposition of hydrogen gas bubbles on the positive electrode, increasing internal resistance.
The coating of zinc plates with mercury to prevent local action by hiding surface impurities.
A chemical substance like manganese dioxide used to oxidize hydrogen gas and eliminate polarization.
